transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, but it's really starting to mess with my job. I'm a construction manager, you know? I've been in the business for years, worked my way up, seen it all. But lately, I’m here because every time I have to get near a scaffold, roof edge, or upper platform now, my head just... it just tells me I’m about to go over. It's like this overwhelming certainty that I'm going to fall, even when I can see the rails are perfectly in place. I mean, I check the safety setups myself, I know the regulations, I know the setup is supposed to be completely safe, but it doesn't matter. The rational part of my brain knows it's fine, but my body just reacts like I'm standing on a tightrope over the Grand Canyon. I start sweating, my heart races, and I just have to get down. It's embarrassing, frankly, having to tell my crew I need to step back when I'm the one supposed to be leading them up there. I never used to be like this, I used to walk the steel like it was a sidewalk, but now... now just looking up at the scaffolding makes my stomach tie itself in knots.
Do you experience this overwhelming fear of falling in other situations where you're not at a construction site?

Well, that's the thing, doc. It's not just the job site. I wish it was just the job site, because then maybe I could just... I don't know, find a desk job or something, even though I'd hate that. But no, it's creeping into everything else. 

Take last weekend, for example. My wife, Sarah, she wanted to go to this new restaurant downtown. It's on the top floor of this high-rise, one of those places with the floor-to-ceiling windows, you know the type? Supposed to be this great romantic view. We get out of the elevator, and I take one look at those windows and I just... I froze. I couldn't go near the edge. I had to ask the hostess to seat us as far away from the glass as possible, right by the kitchen doors. Sarah was so disappointed, and I felt like a complete idiot. 

And it's not just tall buildings, either. We were driving over the bridge the other day—the big suspension bridge on the interstate—and normally I don't even think twice about it. I've driven over it a thousand times. But this time, we got stuck in traffic right in the middle, right at the highest point, and I just started panicking. I gripped the steering wheel so hard my knuckles were white, and I just kept staring straight ahead, terrified that if I looked out the window down at the water, the car would somehow just tip over the edge. I was sweating through my shirt, my chest was tight... I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack right there in the driver's seat. 

Even simple things, like... like going to the mall. They have those glass elevators and the open walkways on the second and third floors looking down at the food court. I can't walk near the railing anymore. I have to hug the wall, walking right past the storefronts, just to feel safe. It's exhausting. It's like my brain is constantly scanning for edges, for drop-offs, and the second it finds one, it just hits the panic button. So yeah, it's definitely not just the scaffolding. It feels like it's everywhere now. I can't even change a lightbulb on a stepladder at home without my knees shaking. It's just... it's ruining my life, honestly.
Do you experience this kind of overwhelming fear or panic in situations that don't involve heights or falling?

No... no, doc, that's the craziest part of all this. It really is. I mean, you'd think if I was just, you know, a nervous guy or losing my nerve in general, I'd be jumping at shadows everywhere, right? But I'm not. I've never been an anxious person. 

You put me in a tight crawlspace under a foundation where you can barely breathe? Fine. No problem. You want me to operate heavy machinery, deal with live wires, handle power tools that could take your arm off if you blink at the wrong time? Doesn't faze me in the slightest. I deal with actual, physical hazards every single day on the site. I've had guys on my crew get into screaming matches, almost coming to blows over material delays, and I'm always the one who steps right in the middle, totally calm, and breaks it up without breaking a sweat. 

My wife, Sarah, she hates spiders and bugs. If there's a spider in the garage, she won't go in there until I deal with it. I just scoop it up with my bare hands, toss it outside. Doesn't bother me a bit. Crowds don't bother me. Enclosed spaces don't bother me. I even had to give a speech at my daughter's wedding last year in front of two hundred people, and sure, I had a little butterfly in my stomach, but nothing like this. Nothing like that sheer terror. 

It's literally just the drop. The edge. The distance between me and the ground. If my feet are on solid earth, or if I'm in a room with no windows, I am the calmest, most level-headed guy you'll ever meet. It's so frustrating because I know I can handle stress. I've built my whole career on handling stress! But this... it's like a switch flips in my head and I'm just gone. It just doesn't make any sense to me why my brain would only care about this one specific thing when I deal with dangerous stuff all day long, you know? It's just the heights. Nothing else does this to me.
Is your fear more about the act of falling itself or about being in a high place in general?

Well, doc, that's... that's a really good question, actually. I've been trying to figure that out myself, turning it over in my head when I can't sleep, which is happening more and more lately, to be honest. It's tough to untangle, you know? 

Like, if I'm just standing in a tall building, right? Say I'm in the middle of a room on the fiftieth floor, nowhere near a window. I'm okay. I know I'm high up, my brain registers the elevation, but I'm not panicking. I might feel a little... I don't know, a little on edge, maybe a tiny bit hyper-aware of the fact that there's a lot of empty space beneath the floorboards, but I'm not sweating through my shirt. I can have a conversation, I can do my job. 

But the second I have to get near the edge... that's when it all goes to hell. It's the precipice. It's looking down and seeing the drop. It's this overwhelming, crushing feeling that the ground is pulling me, or that I'm just going to lose my balance and go over. Even when I'm on a scaffold with a guardrail that I personally inspected, a rail I know could stop a small truck, my brain just screams, 'You're going over, you're going to fall.' 

So, I guess... I guess it's not just the altitude itself. If I'm enclosed, if I feel secure, the height alone doesn't break me. It's the exposure. It's the vulnerability to the fall. Like with that restaurant I mentioned with Sarah, the height of the building wasn't the problem until I saw those floor-to-ceiling windows and suddenly the drop was right there, right in my face. Or on the site, I can be up on the tenth floor of a framed-out building, but if I have to walk the perimeter where the exterior walls aren't up yet... that's when my legs turn to jelly and I have to crawl on my hands and knees just to get away from the edge. It's the falling. It's the absolute terror of the fall. I just... I can't shake the feeling that the edge is a magnet and I'm just going to get pulled right off it.
